samples.task_summary: Predict elevated blood lead level risk from NHANES participant attributes while favoring signals likely to generalize across survey years and subpopulations.

scores.rationale: Survey year is largely a domain indicator and can capture shifting background lead exposure trends rather than person-level causal risk, so it is brittle for OOD generalization.
Country of birth can relate to environmental exposure history and housing or occupational differences, but it is also a coarse demographic proxy that may shift across domains.
Education is a reasonably stable socioeconomic marker linked to housing quality, occupation, and exposure risk, though some of its signal may come through demographic stratification.
Age is a strong and broadly stable predictor because cumulative exposure, historical exposure environments, and life-stage differences plausibly affect lead burden across domains.
Gender may capture some stable occupational and behavioral exposure differences, but it is a relatively weak shortcut-prone demographic feature.
Marital status is an indirect social correlate with limited direct connection to lead exposure and is likely to be unstable across populations and age structures.
Race/ethnicity can correlate with structural exposure disparities, but it is highly sensitive and often acts as a demographic shortcut whose associations may not transport well OOD.

samples.task_summary: Predict whether an NHANES participant has elevated blood lead, favoring features that reflect durable exposure risk rather than survey-wave or demographic shortcuts.

scores.rationale: Survey year is highly domain-specific and likely captures changing background lead exposure and measurement era, so it is a brittle shortcut for OOD generalization.
Country of birth may correlate with lifetime environmental exposure differences, but it is coarse and can act as a demographic/domain proxy rather than a stable causal signal.
Education is a reasonably stable socioeconomic indicator tied to housing, occupation, and environmental risk, making it moderately useful across domains.
Age is a strong, semantically stable predictor because lead burden and historical exposure opportunities vary systematically over the life course and across birth cohorts.
Gender can reflect stable differences in occupation and exposure patterns, but it is also a broad demographic shortcut with limited specificity.
Marital status may weakly track household and socioeconomic context, but it is indirect, age-confounded, and not a robust exposure mechanism.
Race/ethnicity may correlate with structural exposure disparities, but it is a sensitive proxy that risks encoding domain-specific social patterns rather than transportable causal information.

samples.task_summary: Predict whether an NHANES participant has elevated blood lead level from demographic and socioeconomic information in a way that transfers across survey domains.

scores.rationale: Survey year can track secular changes in environmental lead exposure but is also a strong domain identifier and likely brittle under distribution shift.
Country of birth may relate to lifetime exposure environments and housing or occupational histories, but it is also a coarse demographic proxy and can encode subgroup shortcuts.
Education is a fairly stable socioeconomic indicator linked to housing quality, occupation, and environmental risk, so it should retain moderate predictive value across domains.
Age is a strong and semantically stable predictor because lead burden and exposure history vary systematically over the life course.
Gender may capture some stable differences in occupation or exposure patterns, but effects are indirect and it risks acting as a demographic shortcut.
Marital status is only weakly related through household and socioeconomic context and is likely less stable and more confounded than direct risk factors.
Race and ethnicity can correlate with structural exposure disparities, but it is a sensitive attribute with substantial shortcut risk and potentially unstable domain-specific associations.
